statement: Nojpetén (also called Tayasal/Noh Peten), capital of the Itza Maya on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, northern Guatemala, fell 13 March 1697 to a 235-man Spanish force under Martín de Ursúa, governor of Yucatán — this is the last independent, unconquered native kingdom in the Americas, falling 165 years after the 1532 conquest of the Inca and 176 years after the 1521 fall of Tenochtitlan, a real, documented fact frequently omitted from popular narratives that treat "the conquest" as a single rapid event. Grant D. Jones, The Conquest of the Last Maya Kingdom (Stanford University Press), is the standard scholarly treatment.

sources.citation: Jones, Grant D. The Conquest of the Last Maya Kingdom. Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1998.
sources.author: Grant D. Jones

does_not_demonstrate: That Maya political independence ended with the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires, as opposed to persisting in the northern Petén for over 165 additional years
